blocks.x: Yeah? What am I supposed to be ready for? Oh, we're supposed to, uh...

Are you going to ask me some questions? Is that what it is? Oh, yes, and we can, uh... We can put our names on here. Just again, just so we'll know who it is. I've got a whole pocket full of questions here. Ah! Ah! Oh, you want to read that over and sign it? That's plenty enough for me. Okay, here, let me give you something to write on.
Yeah, right there.

Yeah. Yeah. That's all I wanted. I wanted... I just wanted clearance on it. Oh, sure. Well, I can understand. The union has always given us permission. Dave has always been very cooperative. I think Dave is very intelligent.
Dave is one of the finest men, you know. He lost the election on an international board member, vice president of the international union. He lost that.
They stole a march on him, I heard. Sure. They really got him.
Oh, the woods are full of dirty members of organizations.
I've heard that myself on occasion.

Well, I can tell you, they'll never replace him. Oh, no. One of the finest men that I've met in my life. Absolutely impossible to intimidate him in any way whatsoever. But he's complete honesty. I've known Dave so many, many, many years. No one could ever, ever, ever intimidate a man. Okay, what do you want?

I was thinking about different customs that they have, something I haven't asked enough about. You're talking about dressing in tuxes and batwing collars. When you got started, did they allow smoking on the stand? I mean, straight cigarettes.
We never did think of smoking on the stand.
No, you wouldn't. No. Is it allowed now?

Some places, yes. Some places, no. Naturally, I have no way of commenting on it anymore because I just don't smoke. I haven't smoked in 22 years. Really? I haven't touched one of any kind. My goodness.
So you don't think about it when you go to the country clubs, say.
I don't give it a thought. But I have seen some musicians do those things. When I was with Sharky on the bandstand at the famous door, we did not smoke.
Ever.
At the Blue Room, of course, we didn't smoke on the bandstand while working.
Did anybody drink on the bandstand with Sharky's band?
No. During the missions, we all did, with the exception of Sharky. Maybe he had a beer once in a while, but Sharky never did drink. I never did see Sharky drink a high ball in my life.
Did Monk Hazel drink?

Ha! Monk inhaled. Monk used the excuse that he was an alcoholic because his father was an alcoholic and he inherited it from his father. Yet his father was supposed to have become an alcoholic after Monk was born. How could Monk have inherited that from his father? I'll never know. But excuses are excuses are excuses.
Maybe his father inherited it from Monk.
Could. If he was around Monk enough. But I can tell you one thing about Monk.
Yeah.
If Monk ever borrowed money from you, no matter how drunk he was, he always paid it back and he always remembered that he owed it to you. That's right.
Bless his heart.
I've had Monk borrow money from me and pay me back when I was too drunk to remember him even loaned it to him.

Well, he... I remember when I first met him in 1945, he would take a few and he's supposed to have fallen asleep. He told me all kinds of stories about his own drinking. He never told me about falling in the ice trough at the famous store.
Well, I've seen him at the blue room swing at a cymbal with his stick while we were playing and fall off the drums onto the floor. I saw that with my own eyes.
But the management in some places really would object to your drinking, in other words, is really what I'm getting at.
Never unless we got loaded. Yeah.
But, I mean, you didn't take a drink and put it on top of the piano or anything like that.
No, sir. Not at the famous door. We didn't... Well, we had 20 minutes out of each hour in which to drink if we wanted to. But the monk's trouble was that monk would come to work drunk.
Mm-hmm.
And none of the rest of us ever did that.
Yeah. Oh, God. Well, anyway, what was it like traveling? You traveled to a few places. Did you do a lot of one-night stands, stay traveling?
No. Not with Sharky, you mean, or did I?
With any... Oh, yes, I have plenty. Plenty, plenty. Plenty, plenty. Mm-hmm.
I ate sandwiches, ham sandwiches on Christmas Day and turkey on the 4th of July. It's all according to the circumstances.
Mm-hmm.
I've had one-night stands and all over northeast Texas and everything. Austin, San Antonio, not San Antonio, San Angelo.
Mm-hmm.

Kilgore, Texas, Tyler, Texas, Plainview, Texas. My goodness. Dallas, Austin, uh, uh, I don't know, Marshall, Texas, Beaumont. I've even traveled from here and played a job at Beaumont and traveled back home the next day as far as that's concerned.
What band were you with when you did that?
I had my own band.
Mm-hmm.
Who was in it? Tony Fougerette was in it. Uh, sometimes Harry Shields.
Mm-hmm.

It's awfully hard. Billy Neubreger sometimes. Mm-hmm. It's awfully hard to remember who played, uh, who played what instrument at those particular times because there were so many changes. Charlie DuPont, a lot of times, was on the road with me.
What did he play then?
Charlie DuPont played, uh, trumpet. That's Ronnie DuPont's father. Yeah.
But I, uh, I have seen him play bass.

Yeah, well, he... But I don't know how much. He never was a good bass player because he never, he didn't do anything but pick it up and start fooling with it and think he could play. That's the way plenty of them are today. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. They got bass players today that don't even know how to tune the instrument, much less play them and get up there and take somebody else's place and that's the one thing about the union that I never did appreciate. And if you know, you know, I think, as well as I do who it is. Well,
uh, no comment. We won't mention any names.
No,
we won't mention any names. But, well, some people get, get to be band leaders. They should have a baton.
Instead of an instrument.
Yeah.

I don't think that any, any, any union local ought to permit any man to take an instrument and put it on the bandstand and knock somebody else that out of work when he cannot play himself and he sits up there and picks on the instrument or, uh, and, uh, and absolutely picks nothing correctly.
Well, now how does that work? How do you get union leadership?
Well, they, as a general rule, are the leaders.
Well, to get into the union, into the musician's union, what credentials do you have to bring?

To get into the musician's union, according to me, you must be able to play. You must be able to qualify by playing. But it did not happen in a couple of instances. And only one instance in this local can I mention, can I name where this happened. And he, this guy was supposed to be a band leader and he booked a lot of jobs and he made a lot of money for other musicians as well as for himself. But at the same time, I don't think that he should have been allowed ever at any time, regardless of who worked with him or what have you, that he should take an instrument and sit on the bandstand and fake the fact that he's playing when he absolutely is not playing. and some other musician that can play that same instrument does not have a job.
Right.
Because that's, this is a federation of musicians. That particular fellow that I have in mind once tried to give an audition to the New Orleans Symphony. he's that stupid.
Johnny Wiggs told me that he'd call up the Jung Hotel and criticize the band there. Tell them what was wrong with the band. That he thought he knew it.
Do you know who I'm talking about?
Yeah, he knew everything that there was to know. Yeah. I guess that was when Johnny was there with L.A. Stratocos or something.
It's possible.
Incredible story.
Yeah.
That this man just knows it all.
And he knows absolutely nothing.
Yeah.
Except that he was a hustler. He did work at getting jobs.
But how many band leaders, would you say the majority of band leaders are good musicians? Oh, yes.
The majority of them. Oh, yes.
Oh, yes. They're not just guys that hustle up jobs.

This boy that's at the Blue Room right now is one of the finest musicians in the United States or in the world, the band leader. You can tell by the quality of band that he's got. He's got the finest band today. I can't think of his name. He's got the finest band that the Blue Room has ever had as a staff band. And better than most of the other bands that came in that were named bands. Because I have had the pleasure of sitting down and listening to his band.
What does he play himself?
I don't know if it's not violin. Yeah. Yes, it's violin. That's right.
I remember now. Bill Clifford. Yeah.
Bill Clifford. Bill Clifford.
Yeah.

And a very fine person. Very nice person. Yeah. I saw him a couple of weeks ago. I just met him accidentally. I was playing at the hotel and I happened to come down the elevator after the job was over and he was on the elevator and he smiled and said, hello. I said, hello. I said, you look like a musician. He said, I am. He said, you do too. So we introduced ourselves and I told him that I had played quite a lot in the Blue Room in act bands. And he invited me to come in and listen to him. I told him, I said, I had never heard you a band. And I said, I've been hoping someday to hear your band. He said, well, you're busy right now? I said, no. He said, well, why don't you come on in right now? We're just getting ready to play again. So I went in and I've never heard a finer staff band in the Blue Room nor hardly in any hotel where I've ever played. It was just absolutely beautiful.
Now, what would make you say to him, you said, you look like a musician. He said, you do too.
Well, just because you were wearing a band. We were dressed in tux and everything like that and that's just the way it looked.
I see.
That's a matter of starting a conversation for one thing like, boy, it's raining or it's hot as hell outside. You know, something like that you might say.
Did we give
our names, Pam? Oh, on the tape here, no. I know that you're Dick Allen, you know that I'm Pam Tom.
Is it picking up my voice okay? Uh-huh. Picking up yours? Say, tell me your full name, your real name.
It's not much more than Pam Tom, it's Pamela.
Okay, it picks you up. Yeah. Oh, good. I forgot to do that. And today's date is what day?
The first day of August, 1983. Okay, we've got it identified.
And we're at your house, Jeff.
And that's a fact. Yeah.
Okay. Thank you. Yeah, it was payday,
so we know.
Anyway. Well,
with me, the third day of the month is payday. That's Social Security Day. I see.

Well, anyway, a band like that, see, I happened to have gone there a few Saturdays ago, I guess. And, uh, I didn't know too many people in the hotel band. They weren't musicians that I would know from Bourbon Street.
Well, I knew quite a few of them, but the majority of them, I didn't know myself.
Because,
after all, uh, you don't have much association with those musicians unless they were musicians that have, uh, that you have played with before that have come on in. Now, for instance,
Liston Johnson is there and I played many a job with Liston Johnson. Such guys as that.
He doubles, huh? Liston Johnson.

You mean clarinet and sax? Yes. Yeah, but he plays mostly tenor. He plays fine clarinet, but he plays mostly tenor. He gets a gorgeous tone out of a tenor and he can read anything in the world you put in front of him. He's a very fine musician.
I think they even had flutes there. I don't remember.
Oh, yes. Yes, he plays flute too. Yeah.
And they had Emory Thompson on trumpet.

They had a black piano man that I didn't know, a man up in his 50s. Whereas the last time I was there and I listened to the other band, and what's his name, the band leader before that died? Leon Kellner? No, after Kellner.
Oh, I know. Dick Stabile.
Dick Stabile.
Yeah.

Now, Stabile had a very young pianist, but a black man. Very fine musician. Mm-hmm. To play those kind of things in those bands, they must, by all means, be top quality. Or they cannot do the job. I could never be able to play in that because I don't have the formal training. Mm-hmm. I have the talent, but not the training. Yeah.

Well, they impressed me as having a lot of arrangements where they could do any style. Oh, yes. If you wanted a Tommy Dorsey style. Oh, yes. They got it right away. Well, somehow we got off the subject of traveling. What kind of places did you stay in when you were traveling in Texas? I mean, would you stay in a top quality hotel or whatever you could find?
As a general rule, we stayed in the hotel where we played because that was mostly where we played was in hotels.
Mm-hmm.
That went with the job. Yeah.

You know, Billy Newberger is over there now in Texas in San Antonio. I don't know where he is. Well, I see his son occasionally. I know his son better. His son comes back to work once in a while in New Orleans.
Yeah, I played with Billy Newberger and Shorty Reese before either one of them were married.
Really?
Yeah.
Well, his son, I don't think his son plays music, but he's very interested in it.
I don't know. I don't even know his son.
Yeah. But Billy doesn't play anymore. He just quit in town. He dropped out of the music world.
I have no idea. Yeah.
Yeah. Well, San Antonio is where he's at. And you know who's from over there in Marshall? I guess he was born in Mississippi but moved away like you is Tim Kelly.
Is that where Tim is now? No. Someone was asking me.
No, he's in Jackson. He's retired.
That's what I understand. He was with manager of Whirlines in Jackson. But he grew up in Marshall even though he's from a Mississippi family. Yeah.
And he told me about playing around East Texas and how he went on from there to do everything.
I liked Tim very, very much. He was one fine fellow. Mm-hmm. Still is. Oh, yeah. Tim was a very good friend of Peck Kelly's.
Mm-hmm. Well, they finally put out a record of Peck. I haven't heard it yet.
I'd like to have it.
Yeah.
See, I never heard Peck. I just got a couple, an album, a brand new album of Art Tatum's. Boy, it's a knockout. Really? Boy, he played so, so very beautifully.
Did you know Peck in Texas?
Yes, I met Peck. Oh.

I got to the Southern Nenna Club. I was between trains in Houston. And they wouldn't let, this was just after World War II. They wouldn't let servicemen in unless they had a date. I guess they were afraid I was going to start a fight. Yeah. Or something like that. Well, somebody else did before that, and that's the reason for it all. I think if I'd gone up and explained to them.
Yeah.
That I knew people who knew Peck Kelly and wanted to, had been hearing about him for years. Well, a few years then.

You see, I had a very good friend over in Houston. He was manager of the piano department in Carter Music Company, Skipper Trevathian. Mm-hmm. And Skipper played piano and organ. And whenever I'd go to Houston to play at the Shamrock, well, I'd look up Skipper until Skipper passed away. Mm-hmm.
I don't know too many people over there now in the music business.
I heard one band over there. I don't know anybody in the music business anymore.
Yeah. Over there. Well, they had a good young band to me, to my ear, that was playing a cross between bluegrass and string jazz, you know.
Mm-hmm.
They had that Venuti line quintet of the Hot Jazz Club of France.

Yeah. I knew Venuti. Venuti sent me word just before he died to tell me hello. Mm-hmm. Well, anyway. And I'll never forget Red Nichols. I met him out in California and sat in in his band. And he offered me a job that night. He asked me if I'd feel like settling out in Los Angeles. He said, if you settle out here, I'll give you a job immediately. I love the way you knock a band out. He said, you swing a band. You make a band play. That was very nice. It was a very nice thing for a man to say, especially Red Nichols. I swear that that's the truth on the Bible.
Mm-hmm. And you went out in California, too, then.
Well, I only went out there to play with Sharky at this third Dixieland Jamboree, which I've got in my scrapbook. Incidentally, I've located my scrapbook, if you'd like to see it.
Oh, yeah.
Anyhow, we would like to see that.
Where was this Dixieland Jubilee held?
At Shrine Temple. Let me ask you to get it for me. Okay, we can stop the machine. Darling, would you get that scrapbook for me?
Please forgive it.
It's about, let me see. It's over 40 years old. I thought of many a time that I would do it all over again, but... There's Sharky, isn't it? No.
That's recent.
That's Diana.
Yeah.
No, there's Sharky here.
Yeah. That's got to be him. Nobody else will that dare again. Yeah, there's Sharky. And... All right, now.
Here's the band that I was playing in. Come on, uh... Okay, we'll move all this, John.
I've got all these.
Come on, Pam. Okay. Okay. Yeah. Why don't you turn on that light over there, Dick?
All right, now I'll turn the machine around so you can see... And move the microphone in close. We can see if we're talking loud or not.
This is the little outfit on the... Called the Beverly Hills Orchestra, the Hollywood Scandals.
Mm-hmm.

That's the unit that left the Sanger Theater with my wife in it and the unit that I played for. You remember the boys from Baton Rouge that I told you? Fliver Ford. Mm-hmm. Tony Fougerat. Me and Mutt Powers. Mutt's dead. Tony's dead. Fliver's dead. And J.B. I don't know if he's still alive.
That J.B. Landry?
I was 24 years old. J.B. Landry.
On the left.
Yeah.
Fliver Ford next. Then Fougerat. Then you. Yeah. And then Mutt Powers.
This was in 1931.
Well, I would have thought that Mutt Powers would have been short. You could have been Mutt and Jeff then.
We were just about the same band.
Yeah. It had nothing to do with that.
Now, this is the first band at the famous door. Mm-hmm. Santo. And Lester's got his tenor.
Yeah. He's got his clarinet there. Yeah. Yeah. I never saw Chink play tuba there. Did he ever play tuba?
Yeah. Once in a while. He never had a tuba of his own at that time. Yeah. And someone would loan it to him.
And look how differently they're dressed. I mean, that's how I thought bands dressed. But this...
This is in the coca room at the auditorium. That's you. Yeah. Yeah.
Did you play for people getting dressed? For Mardi Gras balls? Ever?
Did I play for them, but they're... For people getting dressed?
In costume. Did you ever hear of that?
No.
Leonard Ferguson was telling me that there's even music.
Well, maybe they did, but I played on Rex Bandwagon four straight...
Oh, yeah. Four straight years.
Now, this is at Blaise D'Antoni's. He's the president of the Standard Fruit Company at the time. This is out at his place, out at River Bend.
Mm-hmm. Is he holding the cup there? Is that a waiter?
That's Blaise. That's Blaise D'Antoni's.
That's Blaise himself. Yeah. Okay. That looks like his...
This is Art Linkletter. Mm-hmm. At Blaise D'Antoni's. That's Blaise.
Mm-hmm.
Mildred, Sharky's wife.
Mm-hmm.
Somebody asked me the other night if she was... She's still alive. I said, sure she is.
Yeah. I saw her on the main, mate. And it's your same... Sharky band. Yeah. And Monk's got his mellophone on it.
Yeah.
Oh, great.
This is in the coca room at the auditorium. Mm-hmm.
Monk has three cymbals. And one cowbell, huh? Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. That... His drum has got two mufflers on it, or whatever you call them.
This is at the famous door.
Monk used brushes.
Oh, brushes everything. Yeah.
And that's Jackie Blaine, huh?
That's Jackie Blaine. Yeah. What became of her, I do not know. Yeah, that's a weirdo. But she was quite a fine little singer. Mm-hmm.
And you've got... You've got the date on this, uh, clipping.
Yeah, September 1948.
The 20th, Monday.
Mm-hmm. It started.
Maybe that's the opening thing.
I don't know.
Yeah. Well, we can check the newspapers now that we've got the date. Smiley Joe, they've got.
It should be Smiley. Yeah, of course. Yeah. Pleasant Joseph is his real name.
And H-Y-P is the way they spell hip.
Yeah.
Hip. Hipolite.
His name, he... Hipolite. Yeah. Hipolite. Gunman.
Somebody told me he used to be a cab driver years ago.
He was, before he'd go in and to the famous door. Mm-hmm. You know, he couldn't knock two nickels together until he married Jenny.
Mm-hmm. Let's get that dog hair off. Yeah, okay. I think we've got it flat on.
Now, this is... This is... I don't know how long we had been playing one year when this picture was... In here. In the famous door. Mm-hmm. Because it was... Much more... Much less elaborate.
Mm-hmm.
Than it was at this time. That was after it was renovated once.
A lot of plush. Yeah. And here we've got you from WDSU program schedule. Yeah. Prepared week of July the 10th, 1949. Yeah. Yeah.

But this was not at WDSU. Mm-hmm. Because the bandstand at WDSU. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. The piano was over here and my back was to the rest of the musicians. Yeah. And I remember just as plain as day. And it was up on the... One of the top stories of the Habana Bank. Mm-hmm.
Let's see. It says jazz by Sharpie. 4 to 4.30 p.m. Sunday.
Mm-hmm. Well, you see... Mm-hmm. See, this was not WDSU. It was broadcast at that time by WDSU. Yeah. But this is at the... At the coca room of the Municipal Artorium.
Where the photo was made, I see. Yes. Yeah. It says available for sponsorship.
Yeah. This is... This is... Kings of Dixieland recommend King Band Instruments. Mm-hmm. This is a sponsorship by Philip Wehrlein.
Mm-hmm. And that's Sunday, April 3rd, 1949. Yeah. 3 to 6 p.m. No.
It's gotta be somewhere...
He always wore that hat. That must have been sort of a signature hat.
Dr. Joseph D'Antoni...
Mm-hmm.
...gave Sharpie this particular derby.
Mm-hmm.

That was a Cavanaugh. One of the top quality derbies. He bought it in New York City and gave it to him. Blaze D'Antoni gave Sharpie his King Trumpet. Yeah. It was a gold King Trumpet. Remember I told you how Sharpie used to take that $600... ...gold horn and... Mm-hmm. ...use a... Uh... This is Myra Menville. And her two children at the time. Myra was a very beautiful, beautiful lady... ...and one of the finest women I ever knew.
She loved Sharpie.
Oh, yes.
And she loved to appreciate him more and more...
No.
...as the years got on.
Well, you can thank her for all... ...for... Thank you.
jazz club. And uh... Helen Art. That uh... that article looks like Time Magazine to me.
This could have been. Or a variety. Well it says music at the top. This looks like
the typography or something. Could have been. Yeah well. I've got some other things from variety.

Jazz festival open Thursday. Jazz concerts and... I don't know who this is. That must be... Larry Wilson. Larry Wilson yeah. From WNO. You see this see this job right here? Monk was so drunk on this truck that when he went to get off of there he fell off on the ground. On the street and nearly killed him. What were we all doing? Well we were playing on the street but Monk come on a job. Came on a job drunk. We were balli-hooing a concert at the auditorium that Sunday afternoon.

So you can get used to watching the machine. See if it's picking up. Testing. Yeah. You and Jim have voices that broadcast. Yeah well we got a bow bow on something. Which one? You were talking about Joe Gloriosa when the machine was off. Mmhmm. See the Flamingo Lounge 405 bourbon. Yeah. Bert Adam owned that. Bert Adam. It was Adam. A-D-A-M. They got B-E-R-T. A-D-A-M-S and it's and it was no S. No.

Who was Cecilia Kirsch? Cecilia Kirsch was a fine little singer and she was in love with a boy named Jock Robinson. Jock was playing with a very fine little band over on the Gulf Coast and she married Jock and they had I think four children. When Jock was on his way to St. Thomas Catholic Church in Long Beach when a drunk came along in a speeding automobile and hit him head on, hit his car head on and killed Jock. Killed Jock immediately. Toed him, just tore him all to pieces. The car was going some nearly a hundred miles an hour. But she carried on and she sang still sang with that same band for many many many years after that. She's still living over there. What she's doing I don't know. But I still love her like my own sister. Now this is the original pork chops and kidney stew. What a group. What are they doing there? Dancing. He's down on his knees. Oh yeah. Well that's what part of he was one of the. See, William Manone with Roger. Roger Wolfe. Yeah. This is Roger Wolfe. He was with WDSU. He was a jockey, you see. A disc jockey. We were the first jazz band to ever play in the pops. We were the first jazz band that ever brought the saints and made it popular. The tune, the saints go marching in. However, Louis Armstrong made it. However, Louis Armstrong made a recording of it before we ever played it. In that recording at the very end of it, I will never forget. He said, one never know, do one. Yeah. This is after, in the coca room, after one of our concerts. It was just back to every Sunday. Now this is on a standard food company ship, the Sailing Morning.

You know, I should remember this. Every Saturday morning we played on there. I should remember these Sunday concerts. It says, opening today, Sunday, September 4th, 1949. It's just about the time I came here. It was in the American Legion Crystal Room. 334. Well, that was on Royal Street, yes. But I really don't remember that. Back to corner of Conta. That may have been just before I got here.
Tom, uh, uh, uh, uh, Tommy Griffin. Tom Griffin.
I talked to, uh, Harvey Blackstone, who wrote Bourbon Street Bounce yesterday. Do you remember Bourbon Street Bounce?
I don't know whether I do or not. I can play it in five minutes if, if, uh, if somebody would start it off.
Well, you probably even recorded. Oh, I know I played it many a time. Yeah.
Bourbon Street Parade and Bourbon Street Bounce.
Mm-hmm.
See?
Well, Harvey's over in Tyler now. That's what reminded me of it when you mentioned Tyler, Texas.
Let's hear it again. Curly Lima. Oh, I remember him. Oh, yeah. Curly used to do a lot of writing things for picking of the item. He worked as a bartender. Yes. Curly died of cancer.
And here's him. It looks like an article from, could be from an English magazine. Melody Maker, but I'm not sure.
I can't say.
No. Well, I just know the typeface, you know.
So tiny. Yeah. I don't remember who this man is. I'd have to look. It would take so long. It would take so very long.
Yeah.
Doraine and Ellis. One of the most beautiful teams that you ever want to see. I want to hear.
What did they do?
Sang at the Blue Room. Mm-hmm. Sent me this card. They must be successful.
They're living in Douglas Town.
Yeah. Douglas Town, Long Island, New York. They were man and wife.
Yeah. Well, that was a...
She was a beautiful, beautiful girl. You would think that you were looking at Jeanette MacDonald. You know, she looked very much like her. This is at Blaise D'Antonis. This is at Keesler Field.
Mm-hmm.

I think. Officers Club at the NAS. It's Shipman. This... This... Algears Naval Base. Or... Some... You know, somewhere. I'd have to... I'd have to just go into all of the details to remember where they were. Yeah. This is at Blaise D'Antonis' home. This building was separate from his house. Does he have a swimming pool? This is home. Yeah, yeah. This is swimming pool. Sharky and Alec Templeton. Mm-hmm.
Now, that's on tape. I've heard that on tape.

This was at the auditorium. Sharky and Alec Templeton. Then Templeton... With pork chops and kidney stew. That's when pork chops and kidney stew were at the blue room with us. And Templeton came over that night. We packed the blue room... Wide open.
I mean, it was just bulging. Mm-hmm. And you've got you sitting on the side there. Yeah.
To sit on the same bandstand with Alec Templeton was an honor. I didn't feel ashamed.

Oh, no. I didn't have to. Oh, no. He's quite a classical pianist. I don't think he swung like you did to tell you the truth. No, he didn't play like me. No. He didn't play like him. Joe Reitman. Mm-hmm. So you would naturally know him well.

That was my very dear friend. Joe thought it too well to me. He thought that it was just simply something that a man could sit on and know as many tunes as I knew without music. He couldn't get over that because that wasn't his category, don't you see? No. Now, this is my brother at the blue room when we were playing there.
Mm-hmm.
My brother Tom, my oldest brother. Mm-hmm. Tom's wife. These other people, I don't remember who they are. Now, this is Tom's wife right here.
I found Tom in the city directory, by the way. Tom Riddick. Thomas M. Riddick. Yeah. And he was working at Whirlines as a sales manager.

And generally, how was the food on the road? You mentioned having to eat hot dogs.

If you had the money to spend, you could get anything in the world you wanted for 50 cents. In those days, you paid 50 cents to a dollar for a meal in a country boarding house. And you had more to eat than they got in the blue room today for a dollar. And they had it on a Lazy Susan-like table. Everything was on a separate table that revolved. And all if you wanted, you didn't say, please pass the beans. You just turned the table to where the beans got to you. And you just ate until you couldn't walk. Biscuits and cornbread and steak and chicken and eight or ten different varieties of vegetables and pie. Just everything.
